Memory Jogger.new: The Recess Appointments Clause reaches intra-session as well as inter-session recesses and vacancies that arose before the recess, but a break of fewer than 10 days is presumptively too short, and the Senate is in session when it says it is; so President Obama's January 2012 NLRB appointments, made during a three-day gap between pro forma sessions, were invalid (9--0 in judgment) (\href{https://supreme.justia.com/cases/federal/us/573/513/}{Justia}).

Detailed Case Facts.to: The D.C. Circuit vacated the NLRB order

Procedural History.from: The D.C. Circuit vacated the NLRB order

Judicial Votes.new: The Supreme Court unanimously \textbf{affirmed} the D.C. Circuit's judgment (9--0), though it divided 5--4 on the scope of the Recess Appointments Clause. The case was argued on January 13, 2014, and decided on June 26, 2014 (\href{https://supreme.justia.com/cases/federal/us/573/513/}{Justia}; \href{https://www.law.cornell.edu/supremecourt/text/12-1281}{Cornell LII}):

Examples: Future Applications.new: \item \textbf{Same-Side (Appointment Invalid): Pro Forma Sessions and a Short Holiday Break.}

Examples: Future Applications.from: the Senate convenes every Tuesday and Friday

Examples: Future Applications.new: \item \textbf{Same-Side (Agency Order Void): A Quorum That Depends on an Invalid Appointee.} During a five-day break in the middle of a session, with no pro forma sessions, the President recess-appoints a member to a three-member federal commission that needs two members for a quorum. The new member and one Senate-confirmed member then issue an order fining a shipping company. The company petitions for review, arguing that the commission lacked a quorum. Under \textit{Noel Canning}, a recess of fewer than ten days is presumptively too short, and nothing unusual justified the appointment. The appointee therefore never lawfully held office, the commission acted without a quorum, and---as with the NLRB order against Noel Canning---the order must be set aside (\href{https://supreme.justia.com/cases/federal/us/573/513/}{Justia}).

Examples: Future Applications.from: A Cabinet Secretary resigns on June 1

Examples: Future Applications.new: \item \textbf{Opposite-Side (Appointment Valid): The Break Between Sessions.} The Senate's first session ends on December 20, and the second session is scheduled to begin on January 5; the Senate schedules no pro forma sessions. On December 28, the President recess-appoints an ambassador to a post that has been vacant for eight months because the nomination stalled in committee. Justice Scalia's view that the vacancy must first arise during the recess would doom the appointment, but the majority's holdings sustain it: the Clause covers vacancies that already exist during the recess, and an inter-session recess of more than ten days is long enough to trigger the President's power. The appointee may serve until the end of the Senate's next session.

\item \textbf{Fence-Sitter (Uncertain): A Catastrophe During a Nine-Day Recess.} During a nine-day intra-session recess, a terrorist attack kills the Secretary of Homeland Security and her deputy, and the Senate cannot promptly reconvene. The President recess-appoints a new Secretary. A nine-day break is presumptively too short under \textit{Noel Canning}, but the Court left room for very unusual circumstances such as a national catastrophe, while making clear that Senate political opposition does not qualify. A court would have to decide whether the emergency truly prevented the Senate from acting and whether temporary acting officials could have filled the gap. Because the Court has never applied the exception, the outcome is uncertain.
